# Lift dock tear-out lifecycle with FleetCockpit as first consumer

## Context

Epic `#17539` lifted the shared reducer/projection loop into `Neo.dashboard.DockWorkspace`, then migrated Workstation and the showcase examples. Its reviewed closeout matrix still names O-3 as a blocker: the tear-out/window-lifecycle half has no engine owner and FleetCockpit—the zero-grant host selected as the first consumer—still extends plain `Neo.container.Base`.

The dependency is explicit rather than inferred. Epic neomjs/neo-agent-institution#22’s formal review stops its FleetCockpit decomposition until this O-3 leaf lands, then requires a fresh census; its native subgraph is still empty.

At `origin/dev` `2e1a63cf5c`, `apps/agentos/view/fleet/cockpit/Container.mjs` is 4,085 physical lines / 1,795 code LOC. It repeats the class-owned dock holder loop (`applyDockZoneOperation`, `getDockZoneDocument`, `onDockZoneDocumentChange`, `projectDockModel`, `refreshDockWorkspace`, `onDockCrossZoneDrop`) and keeps the common tear-out mechanics beside product-specific popup and Fleet data behavior.

The full structure map currently fails before output with `Cannot create a string longer than 0x1fffffe8 characters`. Scoped maps succeeded: `src/dashboard` contains 30 files with `DockWorkspace.mjs` at 305 code LOC; the Fleet cockpit folder contains two files, with `Container.mjs` at 1,795 code LOC. No new file or directory is proposed.

## The Problem

The base class owns the in-window reducer and projection transaction, but it stops immediately before the second repeated half: detach placement capture, admitted vessel ownership, exact semantic return, and worker window connect/disconnect routing. Workstation, Demo B, and FleetCockpit each implement those mechanics again.

The duplication is already behaviorally expensive. FleetCockpit cannot adopt the engine holder loop without threading its tear-out state through the existing hooks, so the flagship FM consumer remains on the retired host pattern. Conversely, lifting the whole app methods would be wrong: those methods also contain product policy that the engine must not know—Workstation/Demo B owner grants and staged embodiment, Demo B cross-window targets, and Fleet click-popouts plus owner-held return panes.

The reviewed epic boundary is therefore load-bearing: **the engine owns admission, document mutation, and window lifecycle; the app owns embodiment and grant policy.**

## The Architectural Reality

A current-head three-host body comparison confirms the boundary rather than merely repeating the epic:

- All three capture `{tabsNodeId, index}` before `detachItem`, delete refused captures, and reintegrate through semantic `addTab` with exact-home/fallback behavior.
- All three maintain pre-terminal connections versus post-commit `tearOutPanes`, then reparent the same live pane into the admitted vessel.
- Workstation and Demo B consume owner grants, staged embodiment, native routes, and workspace-target registration; FleetCockpit deliberately has zero grant references and uses `tearOutPaneHandles` / `returningTearOutPanes`.
- Each top-level window handler also owns unrelated product flows. Those branches cannot move into the engine under a generic name.

`DockWorkspace` already provides the required holder hooks: `getDockProjectionOptions`, `getPreservedItemIds`, `beforeRefreshDockWorkspace`, `resolvePane`, and the serialized refresh transaction. The missing addition is a generic tear-out lifecycle with explicit hooks at the policy and live-instance boundaries, not another app helper or a generic `DragZone` change.

## The Fix

1. Extend `Neo.dashboard.DockWorkspace` with the common tear-out state and lifecycle: placement capture/refusal cleanup, admitted connection versus committed ownership, semantic exact-position reintegration, and worker connect/disconnect registration for `vesselFlow=tear-out`.
2. Expose narrow template hooks for app-owned policy and embodiment:
   - optional grant admission/consumption (default no-op for Fleet);
   - live pane resolution/reparenting;
   - observable adopt and return moments;
   - product-owned `openTearOutVessel` / `closeTearOutVessel`;
   - non-tear-out window connect/disconnect continuation.
3. Keep generic lifecycle defaults inert unless a consumer enables dock tear-out through `getDockProjectionOptions`.
4. Migrate FleetCockpit to extend `DockWorkspace` as the first consumer:
   - inherit the holder/projection/cross-zone loop;
   - configure shell index 1 and `flex: 1`;
   - map `syncControlBar`, pane resolution, and preserved detached/torn ids onto existing hooks;
   - retain Fleet click-popout, data, UI, and same-instance `returningTearOutPanes` policy app-side.
5. Remove only the duplicated imports, fields, and methods whose ownership moved. Workstation and Demo B migrations onto the new tear-out half remain separate reversible leaves.

## Decision Record impact

`aligned-with ADR 0029` and the reviewed O-3 boundary on Epic neomjs/neo#17539. No persisted `dockZone.v1`, wire vocabulary, or service topology changes.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `DockWorkspace` owns the common tear-out placement/admission/return/window-lifecycle path without importing any app module or naming a product grant format.
- [ ] The engine path covers terminal-first and connect-first admission, refused detach, wrong host/flow/admission token, pre-terminal disconnect, committed disconnect, and exact-once semantic reintegration.
- [ ] Grant policy, vessel opening/closing, live-pane embodiment, and non-tear-out window branches remain explicit consumer hooks with inert defaults.
- [ ] Adopt and return lifecycle moments are observable, and FleetCockpit proves `#16415`'s same-live-instance return through `returningTearOutPanes`.
- [ ] FleetCockpit extends `DockWorkspace`; the six duplicated holder/projection methods and app-owned preview producer are removed rather than shadowing the engine implementation.
- [ ] Fleet maps its persistent toolbar, shell index, pane resolver, control-bar sync, and detached/torn preservation onto existing `DockWorkspace` hooks with no Fleet-only hook added to the engine.
- [ ] The rendered root keeps both `neo-dock-workspace` and `fm-fleet-cockpit`; the projected `.neo-dashboard` token floor and current light/dark Fleet values remain unchanged.
- [ ] Existing click-popout, gesture tear-out, splitter resize, perspective switch, cross-zone drop, and DockService/NL journeys stay green; the tear-out witness crosses the real gesture threshold.
- [ ] A source mutation that bypasses the engine lifecycle or shadows an inherited holder method turns the focused matrix red.
- [ ] Workstation and Demo B remain behaviorally unchanged and keep their app implementations until their own migration leaves.

## Out of Scope

- Migrating Workstation or Demo B onto the new tear-out lifecycle.
- Cross-window workspace transfer, vessel conversion/parking, click-popout product flows, or a new grant schema.
- Fleet information design, data feeds, SCSS redesign, or pane decomposition.
- Changing `DragZone.proxyParentId`, `DockTearOut` gesture grammar, persisted documents, or `neo.harness.*` wire identifiers.
- Closing Epic neomjs/neo#17539; this leaf discharges O-3 only.

## Avoided Traps

- **Core-only Fleet parent swap.** Leaves O-3's tear-out/window lifecycle owner unresolved and certifies the wrong blocker.
- **Moving whole app window handlers into the engine.** Imports product flows and grant policy into a generic class.
- **One hook per Fleet sequence.** Hook admission requires a named engine lifecycle moment, an inert minimal-consumer default, and product policy left app-side.
- **Recreating panes on return.** Violates the owner-held live-instance law and loses in-flight state.
- **Migrating all three rich hosts in one PR.** Hides behavior changes and destroys independent rollback.

* feat(dashboard): a dock pane pops out through the drag terminal (#17947)

The header action enters the SAME pair the pointer tear-out terminal calls -
onDockTearOutExit then onDockTearOutTerminal - so "one vessel pipeline, one
detach commit path" is provable at the call rather than inspected. Admission,
the exactly-once detachItem commit, the throwing-reducer refusal route and
vessel retirement are inherited, not restated. The only delta from the drag
entry is geometry: a click has no live proxy, so the pane box is measured first
and the vessel opens over it.

Double-gated on enableDockTearOutLifecycle, collapsed at the projection-context
assembly so the adapter stays a pure projector on one flag - which also makes
pop-out a reserved host name exactly when the engine can project it.

Focus and announcement stay host-owned, per the family ruling: the host opened
the vessel through its own admission seam, so only it can honestly promise focus
into that window, and an announcement without a host-owned aria-live region is
theater. The bound is stated in the config jsdoc.

Also fixes a latent defect the pop-out name exposed: the reserved-name guard
derived its opt-in identifier as enableDock + capitalised action name + Action,
which silently produced a config that does not exist for any name that is not
one lowercase word - pop-out yielded enableDockPop-outAction. Each row now
carries the identifier, so the message cannot drift from the real config.

* test(dashboard): pin the pop-out double gate at the Workspace (#17947)

The action opt-in alone must not project: without enableDockTearOutLifecycle
there are no tear-out handlers to dispatch into, so the button would offer a
gesture the workspace cannot perform. The adapter reads one flag and would
happily project on it, so this arm is what holds the gate at the context
assembly where both configs live.

Two of its three assertions were vacuous on the first attempt: tabsOf yields
item IDS rather than tab nodes, so .headerActions was always undefined and both
not.toContain arms passed against an empty array. Only the positive arm exposed
it. Now collected by dockNodeType with an explicit guard that the fixture
projects a tabs node at all.

* test(dashboard): the pop-out click is witnessed on a rendered workspace (#17947)

The AC's gesture-proof guardrail, on the maximize sibling's fixture template: a
real click on the projected action, through the real router, into the tear-out
pair's own commit.

What only a rendered fixture can prove, and the unit layer cannot:

- the vessel request carries the PANE's real laid-out box, with the workspace's
  own box as the discriminating control — a handler measuring the workspace, or
  the tab button, passes every unit assertion and fails here;
- the painted frozen order pin -> pop-out -> maximize -> close, read on the edge
  node because `pin` hides itself where the active item has no owning edge;
- a declined vessel leaves the document byte-identical and the pane docked;
- the item comes home through the engine's own dead-vessel compensation.

Also corrects three contract drifts in the implementation half: the router's
jsdoc named an engine set without `pop-out`, the adapter's reserved-name list
told a host `pop-out` was free while the engine reserves it, and the handler
leaked the seam's bare Boolean where every other row returns {document, errors}.

The AC's `autoHidden`-clears-on-detach clause is deliberately not asserted in
either direction: ADR 0029 section 2.7 states the rule and Operations.detachItem
does not implement it. That gap sits in the shared detach commit, so it reaches
the drag terminal and the keyboard twin identically; filed separately rather
than patched behind a header leaf.

* docs(dashboard): the pop-out option set and the autoHidden note say what is true (#17947)

RA-4, mechanical half. Three documentation surfaces disagreed with the code they
describe, and one of them advertised an assertion the file does not make.

`LayoutAdapter#project` listed `pop-out` in its reserved-name prose but carried no
option row for either `enableDockPopOutAction` or `dockPopOutIconCls`, so the one
option whose reservation is a CONJUNCTION was the one option a consumer could not
look up. `Workspace#getDockProjectionOptions` enumerated close/maximize/pin/reload
and stopped, which reads as "pop-out is a host name" — the exact confusion RA-2
just repaired in code. Both now name it, and both name WHY it differs: the action
dispatches into the tear-out lifecycle, so it is projected only while that is
armed and the name stays free for a host otherwise.

The spec header claimed a `§2.7 mutual exclusion` bullet — "detaching a railed
item clears `autoHidden` in the same commit" — that the file deliberately does not
assert and that is no longer the intended contract. Detachment and auto-hide are
orthogonal states; `detachFromTabs` touching no item field is correct, and the
design record is the side being corrected. The bullet is gone and the in-test note
now says that rather than describing an unresolved divergence.

That left a precondition read with nothing downstream of it, so the arm now
asserts the direction this fixture CAN reach: a sibling's detach commit leaves the
railed item's `autoHidden` exactly as it was. Mutation-verified — flipping the
expectation reds that arm alone; the other four stay green.

* test(dashboard): pop-out teardown arms, and the vessel leak they found (#17947)

RA-3's test half. The click spans two awaits while `destroy()` is synchronous, so
both gaps are reachable in production — the pane is measured through the main
thread, and a host's vessel seam can take arbitrarily long to answer. These arms
drive a REAL `destroy()` into each gap, on the real lifecycle: the stub harness
cannot host them, because `destroy()` only nulls `tearOutHandlers` under
`enableDockTearOutLifecycle`, so a stubbed pair would exercise a teardown that
never happens.

Teardown during MEASUREMENT behaves as designed: the handler refuses before the
seam is called, and no vessel is ever requested for a workspace that is gone.
Mutation-verified — deleting the pre-admission guard reds this arm.

Teardown during ADMISSION does NOT behave as the RA assumed, and the arm reports
what is true rather than what was expected. The coordinator refuses because its
own state was retired underneath it, which reaches the handler indistinguishable
from a host declining the window, so the `destroyed after admission` branch is
never entered — the admission never resolves truthy for it to check. What IS
contractual holds: the path settles as an envelope rather than rejecting (the
projection listener discards this promise, so a rejection would be an unhandled
one in production), and no commit seam is reached.

The arm also found a leak. The host opens a real window, and nothing ever asks it
to close: teardown does not invalidate the coordinator's pending admission, so the
late-vessel retirement path that exists for exactly this case never runs. Measured
across BOTH close collectors — the harness seam and an instance override — each
empty; I checked the second because the first alone could not tell "never closed"
apart from "closed through a seam I was not watching".

That gap is in the shared tear-out machine and the drag gesture reaches it the
same way, so it predates this leaf and is not this leaf's to repair. It is pinned
as an explicit TRIPWIRE asserting the CURRENT behaviour, marked as a leak rather
than as intent: when the follow-up lands, this assertion goes red and must become
the exactly-once close it should always have been. A leak nobody can silently keep.

Local: 59/59 DockWorkspace unit green, check-ticket-archaeology 0 violations.

* fix(dashboard): a late admission closes its vessel, and a refusal stays a refusal (#17947)

Discharges RA-1, RA-3 and RA-4 from the #17970 round-1 review.

RA-3 — the leak the teardown arm pinned is real and it is the workspace's own.
`retireTearOutState` sweeps vessels by `windowName`, and a pending admission has
none yet: the host is still deciding. The sweep skips the record, the host then
answers with a real OS window, and every map that could have named it is gone.
`acquireTearOutVessel` now refuses on a destroyed workspace and closes that
vessel exactly once — through the hook captured BEFORE the await, because
`Neo.core.Base#destroy` deletes own properties and a per-instance consumer hook
read after the await is already gone. The tripwire becomes the exactly-once
close it was pinned to become.

RA-1 — the sibling stub injects `terminalResult: false`, a grammar the real
terminal never emits: on a reducer refusal it returns `retireVessel(vessel)`,
which is ALSO true when the retirement succeeds. The new arm drives the real
pair and asserts the Boolean was genuinely `true` while the caller still gets a
refusal envelope, zero document sync, one retired vessel and no placement record.

RA-4 — the last stale comment: detachment preserves `autoHidden` (#17969), it
does not clear it.
